lesson.title: One Niche, One Species: The Competitive Exclusion Principle
lesson.summary: The competitive exclusion principle states that two species competing for the exact same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely; one will eventually outcompete and displace the other unless they differentiate the way they use that resource.
lesson.body:
In the last chapter you saw that competition can be intense when species need the same resource. The competitive exclusion principle takes that idea to its logical conclusion. It states that if two species require exactly the same limiting resource, in exactly the same way, in the same place, they cannot stably coexist over the long term. Even a very small edge, a slightly faster reproductive rate, slightly better efficiency at converting food into offspring, will eventually let one species out-reproduce the other. Given enough time, the less efficient competitor is driven locally extinct. This is sometimes called Gause's principle, after the Russian ecologist Georgii Gause.

Gause demonstrated this experimentally in the 1930s using two species of the single celled protist Paramecium, Paramecium aurelia and Paramecium caudatum. When he grew each species alone in a test tube with a fixed daily supply of bacteria as food, both populations grew well and leveled off at a stable size. But when he grew the two species together in the same tube, the outcome was very different. Paramecium aurelia consistently reproduced faster and used the bacterial food supply more efficiently, and within about two weeks it drove Paramecium caudatum toward extinction in that culture. The two species were, in that experimental setup, competing for the identical resource in the identical way, and the principle held: one species was excluded.

It is worth being precise about what this principle does and does not claim. It is a statement about species that occupy the same ecological niche in the strict sense of requiring the same limiting resource in the same way. It does not say that any two species that merely resemble each other, or that merely eat somewhat similar food, must always exclude one another. Real environments are also more complicated than a test tube: conditions fluctuate, predators and disease intervene, and resources vary across space and time, all of which can slow exclusion down or prevent it from ever fully playing out. Still, as a theoretical baseline the principle is one of the most important ideas in ecology, because it makes a strong prediction: long term, stable coexistence between competitors requires some kind of difference between them.

That prediction turns out to matter enormously for understanding real communities, because in nature we constantly see similar species living side by side rather than one eliminating the other. If the competitive exclusion principle is correct, then that coexistence has to be explained somehow. Either the resource is not actually identical for both species, or the species have found some way to split it up. That splitting up of resources is called resource partitioning, and it is the subject of the next chapter.
